title: +50% or -40%: a winning bet?
hook: Each round averages a 5% gain. Play 100 rounds and you should get rich. Do you?

knows: expected value of a simple bet
doesNotKnow: that compounding bets are judged by the typical (geometric) outcome, not the average
that a mean can be carried by a few lucky players

misconception: A bet with a positive expected return per round makes you richer over time.
objective: The learner can explain that with multiplying bets the typical player is governed by the product of factors (1.5 x 0.6 = 0.9 per head-tail pair), so most players shrink even though the average across players grows, carried by a few.

claims.text: The average round multiplies money by 1.05, a 5% gain: (1.5 + 0.6) / 2.
claims.source: Arithmetic mean of the two equally likely factors; meanFactor in src/demos/probability/plus-fifty-minus-forty/model.ts. Over 100 rounds the expected wealth is 1.05^100 = 131.5 times the start ($13,150 from $100).

claims.text: A head followed by a tail multiplies money by 0.9, so the typical round multiplies it by the square root of 0.9, about 0.949.
claims.source: 1.5 x 0.6 = 0.9; geometric mean sqrt(0.9) = 0.9487 (typicalFactor in model.ts).

claims.text: A player needs at least 56 heads in 100 rounds to end above the start, and only about 14% of players get them.
claims.source: 1.5^k x 0.6^(100-k) > 1 iff k > 55.75; P(Bin(100, 0.5) >= 56) = 0.1356 (headsToGain(), pAtLeast() in model.ts).

claims.text: The median player after 100 rounds holds about 0.5% of the start ($0.52 of $100).
claims.source: Median outcome has 50 heads and 50 tails: 0.9^50 = 0.00515 (medianAt() in model.ts).

claims.text: On the stage's first 50 players, the typical player ended at $1.29, 8 of 50 ended above $100, and their average was $430.
claims.source: paths() in model.ts, seed 1505, untuned (the first seed tried). Over 500 other batches of 50: players above start ranged 1-14 (median 7), the batch median $0.08-$3.22 (middle 95%), and the batch average exceeded $100 in 82% of batches.

claims.text: This is a toy bet chosen to separate the average from the typical outcome.
claims.source: O. Peters (2019), The ergodicity problem in economics, Nature Physics 15: 1216-1221 (uses this coin game).

recall.question: A fund gains 60% in good years and loses 50% in bad years, equally often. Its average year is +5%. What happens to a typical investor over 20 years?
recall.why: A good year and a bad year multiply money by 1.6 x 0.5 = 0.8. The typical path has as many good as bad years, so it shrinks, even though the average over all investors grows.
